result: The authors developed a novel barcoding method to link viral transcription and progeny production at the single-cell level. Random nucleotide barcodes were inserted near the 3' end of influenza HA and NA genes using a duplicated packaging signal scheme, allowing standard 3' single-cell RNA sequencing to capture both viral transcripts and barcodes. The barcoded viruses grew to similar titers as unmodified viruses, showed no selection for particular barcode sequences across passages, and maintained high barcode diversity (>96% unique in samples of 1500 barcodes, >92% in 4000 barcodes).
evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly praised the method as 'novel' and 'compelling.' The editor states the method is 'novel, compelling' and the anonymous reviewer describes it as 'very well written' with 'experimental choices very well justified' and 'methods very detailed.' The reviewers note that 'experimental caveats, such as PCR cross-overs in next-generation sequencing and cell multiplets in single-cell sequencing, were well accounted for.'

result: Viral transcription and progeny production are poorly correlated in single influenza-infected cells. At low MOI, cells with >25% viral mRNA produce no detectable progeny, while most progeny come from cells with moderate transcription. At high MOI, progeny are produced throughout the transcription range but with no trend for high-transcribing cells to produce more progeny. Overall, viral transcription is a poor predictor of progeny contribution.
evaluation: The editor explicitly states this is a 'major finding' that 'there is a poor correlation between viral transcription levels and progeny virion production at the single-cell level.' The anonymous reviewer identifies this as one of the 'major findings of this study' and notes 'the conclusions are very well supported by the data.' No concerns are raised about this central finding.

result: Cells with extremely high viral transcription often fail to express the NS gene and represent non-productive infections. At both MOI conditions, many of the highest transcribing cells lack NS expression, and mean viral transcription is significantly higher (p<0.01) in NS-negative cells. This suggests NS acts as a negative regulator of viral transcription, consistent with NEP's known role in exporting viral ribonucleoproteins from the nucleus.
evaluation: The editor notes that 'cells in which viral RNAs are transcribed at high levels are not necessarily those producing the most progeny virions,' implicitly accepting this finding. The anonymous reviewer does not challenge this result and instead notes 'the conclusions are very well supported by the data.' The biological interpretation linking NS absence to high transcription is presented with supporting citations and is not questioned by reviewers.

result: Progeny production is even more heterogeneous than viral transcription in single cells. At low MOI, nearly half of infected cells produce no detectable progeny, while a few cells each generate >10% of all progeny. Gini coefficients for progeny production (0.78-0.88) exceed those for transcription (0.40-0.46). Just 6 of 91 cells account for half the physical progeny at low MOI, compared to 23 cells for half the transcripts.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly identifies this as a 'major finding' that 'progeny virion production is also very heterogenous, i.e., a few cells produce most of the progeny virions.' The editor's summary also emphasizes this heterogeneity. The quantitative measures (Gini coefficients, cell counts) are not questioned by reviewers.

result: Only some of the discrepancy between transcription and progeny production can be explained by viral gene absence or mutations. Progeny production remains highly variable even among cells with complete unmutated genomes, suggesting cellular or uncharacterized viral factors also contribute to heterogeneity.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer notes 'the conclusions are very well supported by the data' and does not challenge this finding. The reviewer does request 'additional speculations about viral or cellular factors (e.g. differences in innate immune responses, differences in cell division status) that might explain the observed heterogeneity,' which acknowledges the validity of the finding while requesting more discussion of potential mechanisms.

result: Under both infection conditions, there was extremely wide variation in viral transcription among infected cells. In most cells, viral transcripts accounted for <10% of all transcripts, but in some cells over half were viral. At low MOI, ~40% of cells failed to express all eight viral genes, with fewer failures at high MOI likely due to complementation. Each viral gene showed variable absence rates across cells.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer notes that 'observations that viral transcription levels are very heterogenous at the single-cell level are not novel, but reinforce those from previous studies.' This indicates acceptance of the findings while noting they confirm prior work. The editor does not raise concerns about these observations.

result: Complete viral genome sequences were obtained for 131 of 254 infected cells at low MOI. About a third expressed all eight genes without non-synonymous mutations, while the remainder had missing genes, mutations, or both. Mutated virions most commonly had one mutation, though some had two or three, and some had large internal deletions.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer states 'the conclusions are very well supported by the data' and does not challenge these genomic characterization results. The methods for genome reconstruction are described as 'very detailed' and the reviewer notes that technical caveats were 'well accounted for.'

result: Cells that fail to express any viral gene produce little or no detectable progeny virions, regardless of total viral transcription, presumably because the absence of encoded proteins impairs virion formation. However, cells expressing all viral genes often still fail to produce detectable progeny.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer notes 'the conclusions are very well supported by the data' and does not challenge this finding. The reviewer does note that 'Figure 5C suggests that cells missing the expression of one viral gene might still be able to produce progeny viruses' and requests 'information regarding which gene was not expressed in these cells,' indicating interest in more detailed analysis rather than disagreement with the finding.

result: At low MOI, physical progeny are produced by cells with both mutated and unmutated genomes, but more infectious progeny come from cells with unmutated genomes, likely because some mutations interfere with functions required for infecting new cells. Physical and infectious progeny production are more correlated (R=0.39) than transcription and progeny production (R=-0.14).
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer does not challenge these findings and notes 'the conclusions are very well supported by the data.' The distinction between physical and infectious progeny is part of the novel methodology that reviewers praised.

result: The study has several acknowledged limitations: experiments used a cell line rather than differentiated airway cells, a single H1N1 strain at a single timepoint, and single-cell RNA sequencing captures only a fraction of input cells.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer raises a concern about reproducibility, asking 'How reproducible are the results?' noting 'it seems that the results presented here are from one single experiment.' This suggests uncertainty about whether the findings would replicate across experimental conditions, though the reviewer acknowledges 'the limitations of the study and how those might influence the conclusions are also clearly explained.'

result: In samples of 1500 barcodes, >96% were unique for both HA and NA; in samples of 4000 barcodes, >92% were unique.
evaluation: The anonymous reviewer raises a methodological concern: 'With this information, it should be possible to assess whether non-unique barcodes were detected in infected cells, and if yes, remove these from the downstream analysis.' This suggests the reviewer wants confirmation that non-unique barcodes were properly handled in the analysis, indicating some uncertainty about whether this potential confound was fully addressed.
